claim: Chemotaxis proteins organize into large, highly ordered, chemotactic signaling arrays in Vibrio species that are found at the cell pole.
source: Chemotaxis proteins organize into large, highly ordered, chemotactic signaling arrays, which in Vibrio species are found at the cell pole.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the abstract describing the organization and localization of chemotaxis proteins in Vibrio species.

claim: ParP mediates proper localization of signaling arrays by tethering arrays to a cell pole anchor, ParC.
source: Proper localization of signaling arrays is mediated by ParP, which tethers arrays to a cell pole anchor, ParC.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known function of ParP.

claim: ParP's C-terminus integrates into the core-unit of signaling arrays through interactions with MCP-proteins and CheA.
source: Here we show that ParP's C-terminus integrates into the core-unit of signaling arrays through interactions with MCP-proteins and CheA.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: ParP's intercalation within core-units stimulates array formation.
source: Its intercalation within core-units stimulates array formation, whereas its N-terminal interaction domain enables polar recruitment of arrays and facilitates its own polar localization.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: ParP's N-terminal interaction domain enables polar recruitment of arrays and facilitates its own polar localization.
source: Its intercalation within core-units stimulates array formation, whereas its N-terminal interaction domain enables polar recruitment of arrays and facilitates its own polar localization.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Linkage of ParP's domains couples array formation and localization and results in controlled array positioning at the cell pole.
source: Linkage of these domains within ParP couples array formation and localization and results in controlled array positioning at the cell pole.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: ParP's integration into arrays modifies its own and ParC's subcellular localization dynamics, promoting their polar retention.
source: Notably, ParP's integration into arrays modifies its own and ParC's subcellular localization dynamics, promoting their polar retention.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by photobleaching experiments in the manuscript.

claim: ParP serves as a critical nexus that regulates the localization dynamics of its network constituents and drives the localized assembly and stability of the chemotactic machinery.
source: ParP serves as a critical nexus that regulates the localization dynamics of its network constituents and drives the localized assembly and stability of the chemotactic machinery, resulting in proper cell pole development.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion stated in the abstract and supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence in the manuscript.

claim: Chemotaxis enables motile bacteria to bias their movement away from unfavorable chemical stimuli and towards more favorable compounds.
source: This process enables motile bacteria to perceive changes in local concentrations of chemicals; as a result, they can bias their movement away from unfavorable chemical stimuli and towards more favorable compounds (Wadhams and Armitage, 2004; Sourjik and Armitage, 2010).
evidence: This is a well-established fact about chemotaxis supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In E. coli, chemotaxis is mediated by an array of highly organized macromolecular complexes built from core chemotaxis units.
source: In the best studied model organism Escherichia coli, chemotaxis is mediated by an array of highly organized macromolecular complexes built from core chemotaxis units.
evidence: This is a well-established fact about E. coli chemotaxis supported by the broader context of the introduction.

claim: The chemotaxis signaling cascade is initiated upon the detection of chemotactic stimuli by methyl-accepting chemotaxis proteins (MCPs).
source: In general, the chemotaxis signaling cascade is initiated upon the detection of chemotactic stimuli by methyl-accepting chemotaxis proteins (MCPs).
evidence: This is a well-established fact about chemotaxis signaling supported by the broader context of the introduction.

claim: MCPs interact with a cytoplasmic histidine kinase, CheA, while the adaptor protein CheW stabilizes this interaction and participates in regulating CheA kinase activity.
source: These membrane-spanning receptors then interact with a cytoplasmic histidine kinase, CheA, while the adaptor protein CheW stabilizes this interaction and participates in regulating CheA kinase activity (Ortega et al., 2013; Parkinson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a well-established fact about chemotaxis signaling supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A phosphosignaling cascade is initiated via CheA and its cognate response regulator CheY.
source: A phosphosignaling cascade is initiated via CheA and its cognate response regulator CheY.
evidence: This is a well-established fact about chemotaxis signaling supported by the broader context of the introduction.

claim: Phosphorylated CheY induces a change in flagellar rotation and consequently in the direction of bacterial swimming, which over time results in net movement towards a more favorable environment.
source: Phosphorylated CheY induces a change in flagellar rotation and consequently in the direction of bacterial swimming, which over time results in net movement towards a more favorable environment (Wadhams and Armitage, 2004; Sourjik and Armitage, 2010).
evidence: This is a well-established fact about chemotaxis signaling supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: MCPs consist of a variable N-terminal extracellular ligand binding domain, a cytoplasmic HAMP domain, and a well conserved signaling domain.
source: MCPs usually consist of a variable N-terminal extracellular ligand binding domain, a cytoplasmic HAMP domain, and a well conserved signaling domain (or kinase control domain) with a highly conserved protein interaction tip that directs the assembly and action of receptor signaling complexes (Figure 1A) (Kim et al., 1999; Falke and Hazelbauer, 2001; Alexander and Zhulin, 2007; Hazelbauer et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a well-established fact about MCP structure supported by citations to previous literature and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The MCP tip contains sites for forming trimers of receptor dimers and for binding to CheA and CheW.
source: Importantly, the tip contains sites for forming trimers of receptor dimers (Kim et al., 1999; Parkinson et al., 2015), and for binding to CheA and CheW (Miller et al., 2006; Park et al., 2006; Vu et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2012; Li et al., 2013; Piasta et al., 2013; Pedetta et al., 2014; Cassidy et al., 2015) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a well-established fact about MCP structure and function supported by multiple citations to previous literature and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: CheA is comprised of five separate domains (P1 to P5) with specific functions.
source: The histidine kinase CheA is comprised of five separate domains (P1 to P5) with specific functions (Figure 1B, green).
evidence: This is a well-established fact about CheA structure supported by the broader context of the introduction and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: CheA P1 is the phosphotransfer domain and contains the substrate histidine for autophosphorylation.
source: P1 is the phosphotransfer domain and contains the substrate histidine for autophosphorylation; P2 binds CheY for phosphotransfer from P1 (Swanson et al., 1993; Morrison and Parkinson, 1994; Bilwes et al., 1999);
evidence: This is a well-established fact about CheA domain function supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CheA P2 binds CheY for phosphotransfer from P1.
source: P1 is the phosphotransfer domain and contains the substrate histidine for autophosphorylation; P2 binds CheY for phosphotransfer from P1 (Swanson et al., 1993; Morrison and Parkinson, 1994; Bilwes et al., 1999);
evidence: This is a well-established fact about CheA domain function supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CheA P3 is the dimerization domain.
source: P3 is the dimerization domain (Park et al., 2006; Cassidy et al., 2015);
evidence: This is a well-established fact about CheA domain function supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CheA P4 is the kinase or ATP binding domain.
source: P4 is the kinase or ATP binding domain;
evidence: This is a well-established fact about CheA domain function supported by the broader context of the introduction.

claim: CheA P5 is an SH3-like regulatory domain, which binds the signaling tip of MCPs.
source: and P5 is an SH3-like regulatory domain, which binds the signaling tip of MCPs (Borkovich et al., 1989; Gegner et al., 1992; Bilwes et al., 1999; Zhao and Parkinson, 2006).
evidence: This is a well-established fact about CheA domain function supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CheW consists of a single SH3-like domain, and is structurally similar to P5 of CheA.
source: The adaptor protein CheW (Figure 1B, red) consists of a single SH3-like domain, and is structurally similar to P5 of CheA (Griswold et al., 2002; Li et al., 2013; Cassidy et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a well-established fact about CheW structure supported by citations to previous literature and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: MCPs, CheA, and CheW form stable core signaling complexes.
source: Together, MCPs, CheA, and CheW form stable core signaling complexes.
evidence: This is a well-established fact about chemotaxis array structure supported by the broader context of the introduction.

claim: One CheA dimer joins two MCP trimer-of-dimers and two CheW proteins in the core signaling complex.
source: As shown in Figure 1B, one CheA dimer joins two MCP trimer-of-dimers and two CheW proteins.
evidence: This is a well-established fact about chemotaxis array structure supported by citations to previous literature and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: The helix formed by the dimerization of the P3 domains of CheA positions itself between the two MCP dimer-of-trimers.
source: The helix formed by the dimerization of the P3 domains of CheA positions itself between the two MCP dimer-of-trimers (Briegel et al., 2011; Li and Hazelbauer, 2011; Briegel et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2012, 2013; Briegel et al., 2014a)
evidence: This is a well-established fact about chemotaxis array structure supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Each P5 domain of a CheA dimer binds to one CheW.
source: and each P5 domain of a CheA dimer binds to one CheW.
evidence: This is a well-established fact about chemotaxis array structure supported by the broader context of the introduction.

claim: A single core unit is arranged in a hexagonal structure held together by contacts between CheA-MCPs, CheW-MCPs and CheA-CheW.
source: Therefore, a single core unit is arranged in a hexagonal structure held together by contacts between: (i) CheA-MCPs, (ii) CheW-MCPs and (iii) CheA-CheW.
evidence: This is a well-established fact about chemotaxis array structure supported by the broader context of the introduction.

claim: Hexagonal core units join to form a super-lattice structure, commonly known as the chemosensory array.
source: According to the current model, further hexagonal core units then join to form a super-lattice structure, commonly known as the chemosensory array (Briegel et al., 2009, 2012; Liu et al., 2012, 2013; Briegel et al., 2014a, 2014b; Piasta and Falke, 2014) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a well-established fact about chemotaxis array structure supported by citations to previous literature and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: CheA-CheW interactions bridge the two receptor trimers of every core and give the array its characteristic stability and high sensitivity.
source: In vivo and in vitro observations indicate that CheA-CheW interactions bridge the two receptor trimers of every core and give the array its characteristic stability and high sensitivity (Zhao and Parkinson, 2006; Hazelbauer et al., 2008; Erbse and Falke, 2009; Briegel et al., 2009; Li and Hazelbauer, 2011; Briegel et al., 2012; Slivka and Falke, 2012; Sourjik and Wingreen, 2012; Liu et al., 2012; Briegel et al., 2014a; Piasta and Falke, 2014).
evidence: This is a well-established fact about chemotaxis array structure and function supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: In E. coli, array formation is thought to be a stochastic process in which individual receptors are inserted randomly in the membrane, and subsequently diffuse freely until they either join existing arrays or nucleate new ones.
source: Here, array formation is thought to be a stochastic process in which individual receptors are inserted randomly in the membrane, and subsequently diffuse freely until they either join existing arrays or nucleate new ones (Thiem and Sourjik, 2008).
evidence: This is a well-established fact about E. coli chemotaxis array formation supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: In E. coli, stochastic array formation results in a non-uniform distribution of signaling arrays at cell poles and randomly along the cell length.
source: This process results in a non-uniform distribution of signaling arrays at cell poles and randomly along the cell length (Sourjik and Berg, 2000), and likely ensures that sensory arrays are in close proximity to the lateral flagella.
evidence: This is a well-established fact about E. coli chemotaxis array localization supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: In organisms such as C. crescentus, P. aeruginosa, R. sphaeroides, and several Vibrio species, chemosensory arrays are actively localized to the cell poles.
source: In organisms such as Caulobacter crescentus, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Rhodobacter sphaeroides, and several Vibrio species, chemosensory arrays are actively localized to the cell poles (Alley et al., 1992; Maddock and Shapiro, 1993; Wadhams et al., 2003; Bardy and Maddock, 2005; Ringgaard et al., 2011; Ringgaard et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a well-established fact about chemotaxis array localization in various organisms supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In V. cholerae and V. parahaemolyticus, chemosensory arrays are exclusively localized at one or both cell poles by a mechanism that depends on the partner proteins ParC and ParP.
source: In the polarly flagellated pathogens Vibrio cholerae and Vibrio parahaemolyticus, we recently reported that chemosensory arrays are exclusively localized at one or both cell poles by a mechanism that depends on the partner proteins ParC and ParP, both of which are encoded within the chemotaxis operon (Ringgaard et al., 2011; Yamaichi et al., 2012; Ringgaard et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a previously reported finding by the authors supported by citations to their previous work.

claim: In V. cholerae, chemotaxis proteins encoded by chemotaxis operon II, e.g. CheA1 and CheW1, are directed to the cell pole by ParC and ParP.
source: For V. cholerae, chemotaxis proteins encoded by chemotaxis operon II, e.g. CheA1 and CheW1, are directed to the cell pole by ParC and ParP (Ringgaard et al., 2015; Briegel et al., 2016), and from here on, CheA and CheW will be used instead of CheA1 and CheW1, respectively.
evidence: This is a previously reported finding by the authors supported by citations to their previous work.

claim: In newborn Vibrio cells, signaling arrays are exclusively localized to the old flagellated cell pole, then recruited to the new cell pole as cells enlarge, resulting in a bi-polar localization pattern.
source: In newborn Vibrio cells, these signaling arrays are exclusively localized to the old flagellated cell pole, then recruited to the new cell pole as cells enlarge, resulting in a bi-polar localization pattern.
evidence: This is a previously reported finding by the authors supported by the broader context of the introduction.

claim: At cell division each daughter cell inherits a signaling array positioned at its old pole.
source: Thus, at cell division each daughter cell inherits a signaling array positioned at its old pole (Ringgaard et al., 2011, 2014).
evidence: This is a previously reported finding by the authors supported by citations to their previous work.

claim: In the absence of either ParC or ParP, the chemotaxis arrays are no longer properly recruited to the cell poles and instead form and localize randomly along the cell length.
source: In the absence of either ParC or ParP, the chemotaxis arrays are no longer properly recruited to the cell poles. Instead, signaling arrays form and localize randomly along the cell length, and bi-polar localization is not established prior to cell division.
evidence: This is a previously reported finding by the authors supported by the broader context of the introduction.

claim: In the absence of ParC or ParP, daughter cells do not faithfully inherit a signaling array at their old poles, resulting in altered motility and decreased chemotaxis.
source: Therefore, daughter cells do not faithfully inherit a signaling array at their old poles, resulting in altered motility and decreased chemotaxis (Ringgaard et al., 2011, 2014).
evidence: This is a previously reported finding by the authors supported by citations to their previous work.

claim: ParC mediates polar localization of ParP.
source: ParC mediates polar localization of ParP, which in turn interacts with a specific domain of CheA that is only present in CheA proteins with an associated ParC/ParP-system (CheA-LID) (Ringgaard et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a previously reported finding by the authors supported by a citation to their previous work.

claim: ParP interacts with a specific domain of CheA (CheA-LID) that is only present in CheA proteins with an associated ParC/ParP-system.
source: ParC mediates polar localization of ParP, which in turn interacts with a specific domain of CheA that is only present in CheA proteins with an associated ParC/ParP-system (CheA-LID) (Ringgaard et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a previously reported finding by the authors supported by a citation to their previous work.

claim: ParP prevents dissociation of CheA from chemotaxis arrays.
source: ParP prevents dissociation of CheA from chemotaxis arrays and disruption of either ParP-ParC or ParP-CheA interactions results in defective recruitment of chemotaxis arrays to the cell poles, leading to their random instead of polar localization (Ringgaard et al., 2011, 2014).
evidence: This is a previously reported finding by the authors supported by citations to their previous work.

claim: Disruption of either ParP-ParC or ParP-CheA interactions results in defective recruitment of chemotaxis arrays to the cell poles, leading to their random instead of polar localization.
source: ParP prevents dissociation of CheA from chemotaxis arrays and disruption of either ParP-ParC or ParP-CheA interactions results in defective recruitment of chemotaxis arrays to the cell poles, leading to their random instead of polar localization (Ringgaard et al., 2011, 2014).
evidence: This is a previously reported finding by the authors supported by citations to their previous work.

claim: In wild-type V. cholerae cells, YFP-CheW1 mainly localized in clusters at the cell poles.
source: In wild-type cells YFP-CheW1 mainly localized in clusters at the cell poles (Figure 1C–E).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the microscopy experiments shown in Figure 1C-E.

claim: In the absence of ParP, YFP-CheW1 clusters were not recruited to the cell poles, but were instead mislocalized along the cell length or completely absent in 74% of cells.
source: In contrast to localization in wild-type cells, in the absence of ParP, YFP-CheW1 clusters were not recruited to the cell poles, but were instead mislocalized along the cell length or completely absent in 74% of cells (Figure 1C–E).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the microscopy experiments shown in Figure 1C-E.

claim: In a strain lacking cheA1, YFP-CheW1 still formed clusters at the cells poles in a manner indistinguishable to that observed in wild-type cells.
source: In a strain lacking cheA1, YFP-CheW1 still formed clusters at the cells poles in a manner indistinguishable to that observed in wild-type cells (Figure 1C–E), suggesting that chemotaxis arrays still form in the absence of CheA.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the microscopy experiments shown in Figure 1C-E.

claim: Chemotaxis arrays still form in the absence of CheA.
source: In a strain lacking cheA1, YFP-CheW1 still formed clusters at the cells poles in a manner indistinguishable to that observed in wild-type cells (Figure 1C–E), suggesting that chemotaxis arrays still form in the absence of CheA.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that YFP-CheW1 still forms polar clusters in the absence of CheA, supported by microscopy data in Figure 1C-E.

claim: For both wild-type and ΔcheA strains, chemotaxis arrays were detectable and indistinguishable in structure by cryo-EM, consisting of an inner membrane-anchored array of MCP proteins and an associated cytosolic baseplate.
source: For both strains, chemotaxis arrays were detectable and indistinguishable in structure, consisting of an inner membrane-anchored array of MCP proteins and an associated cytosolic baseplate.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the cryo-EM experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Out of 61 cells imaged with cryo-EM for each strain, there was a 60% reduction in the number of cells with observable arrays in the ΔcheA background compared to wild-type.
source: Out of 61 cells imaged with cryo-EM for each strain, there was a 60% reduction in the number of cells with observable arrays in the ΔcheA background compared to wild-type – consistent with a role of CheA in stimulating array formation.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the cryo-EM experiments.

claim: The 60% reduction in cells with observable arrays in the ΔcheA background is consistent with a role of CheA in stimulating array formation.
source: Out of 61 cells imaged with cryo-EM for each strain, there was a 60% reduction in the number of cells with observable arrays in the ΔcheA background compared to wild-type – consistent with a role of CheA in stimulating array formation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the quantitative observation from the cryo-EM experiments.

claim: Ordered signaling arrays can still form in the absence of CheA.
source: However, the cryo-EM experiments reveal that ordered signaling arrays can still form in the absence of CheA.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the cryo-EM observations.

claim: In the double deletion strain ∆cheA1 ∆parP, YFP-CheW1 did not form clusters but was localized diffusely in the cytoplasm.
source: Strikingly, in the double deletion strain ∆cheA1 ∆parP, YFP-CheW1 did not form clusters but was localized diffusely in the cytoplasm (Figure 1CE, bottom).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the microscopy experiments shown in Figure 1C-E.

claim: The difference in localization of YFP-CheW1 was not due to differences in expression levels or cleavage of the YFP moiety from the YFP-CheW1 fusion construct.
source: Immunoblot analysis showed that the difference in localization of YFP-CheW1 was not due to differences in expression levels or cleavage of the YFP moiety from the YFP-CheW1 fusion construct (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Formation of signaling arrays is severely compromised in the absence of both ParP and CheA.
source: These data indicate that formation of signaling arrays is severely compromised in the absence of both ParP and CheA, and that CheW1 alone only has a minor effect on array formation but requires the presence of either ParP or CheA, which individually are sufficient for promoting array formation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the microscopy and cryo-EM observations.

claim: CheW1 alone only has a minor effect on array formation but requires the presence of either ParP or CheA, which individually are sufficient for promoting array formation.
source: These data indicate that formation of signaling arrays is severely compromised in the absence of both ParP and CheA, and that CheW1 alone only has a minor effect on array formation but requires the presence of either ParP or CheA, which individually are sufficient for promoting array formation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the microscopy and cryo-EM observations.

claim: In the ∆cheA1 ∆parP strain, out of 61 imaged cells there was an 85% reduction in the number of cells with detectable signaling arrays compared to wild-type.
source: These data are supported by cryo-EM analyses of the ∆cheA1 ∆parP strain, in which out of 61 imaged cells there was an 85% reduction in the number of cells with detectable signaling arrays compared to wild-type.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the cryo-EM experiments.

claim: ParP participates in the process of array formation in addition to its previously known function in promoting polar localization of signaling arrays.
source: Together, these observations suggest that ParP participates in the process of array formation in addition to its previously known function in promoting polar localization of signaling arrays.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the microscopy and cryo-EM observations.

claim: Of the 100 blue colonies sequenced in the bacterial-two-hybrid screen, 95 contained plasmids with genes encoding MCP proteins, corresponding to 15 distinct MCPs.
source: Of the 100 blue colonies sequenced, 95 contained plasmids with genes encoding MCP proteins, corresponding to 15 distinct MCPs (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the bacterial-two-hybrid screen shown in Figure 2B.

claim: All hits in the bacterial-two-hybrid screen included the regions encoding the signaling domains of the MCP proteins.
source: While the fragments of all the mcp genes hit in the screen covered varying regions of the respective genes, all hits included the regions encoding the signaling domains of the MCP proteins.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the bacterial-two-hybrid screen.

claim: All four MCP signaling domains tested interacted with ParP.
source: All four MCP signaling domains interacted with ParP (Figure 2C), confirming that MCPs are a newly identified ParP interaction partner and that interaction occurs via the MCP signaling domain.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the bacterial-two-hybrid experiments shown in Figure 2C.

claim: MCPs are a newly identified ParP interaction partner and interaction occurs via the MCP signaling domain.
source: All four MCP signaling domains interacted with ParP (Figure 2C), confirming that MCPs are a newly identified ParP interaction partner and that interaction occurs via the MCP signaling domain.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the bacterial-two-hybrid experiments shown in Figure 2C.

claim: No interaction between ParC and MCPs was observed.
source: No interaction between ParC and MCPs was observed, suggesting only ParP, but not ParC interacts with MCP proteins.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the bacterial-two-hybrid experiments.

claim: Only ParP, but not ParC interacts with MCP proteins.
source: No interaction between ParC and MCPs was observed, suggesting only ParP, but not ParC interacts with MCP proteins.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the bacterial-two-hybrid experiments.

claim: When YFP-ParP was co-expressed with mCherry-MCP, YFP-ParP also localized in clusters that always co-localized with mCherry-MCP clusters.
source: Strikingly, when YFP-ParP was co-expressed with mCherry-MCP, YFP-ParP also localized in clusters that always co-localized with mCherry-MCP clusters (Figure 2D–E).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the microscopy experiments shown in Figure 2D-E.

claim: ParP interacts with both CheA and MCPs.
source: Therefore, in addition to interacting with CheA and ParC, ParP also interacts (likely in a direct fashion) with MCP proteins. Since ParP interacts with both CheA and MCPs, we hypothesize that ParP forms part of the core chemotaxis unit.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the bacterial-two-hybrid and co-localization experiments.

claim: ParP forms part of the core chemotaxis unit.
source: Therefore, in addition to interacting with CheA and ParC, ParP also interacts (likely in a direct fashion) with MCP proteins. Since ParP interacts with both CheA and MCPs, we hypothesize that ParP forms part of the core chemotaxis unit.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observation that ParP interacts with both CheA and MCPs.

claim: The C-terminal part of ParP consists of a predicted SH3-like domain similar to CheW and the P5 domain of CheA.
source: Interestingly, the C-terminal part of ParP consists of a predicted SH3-like domain (hereafter named array integration and formation domain – AIF domain) similar to CheW and the P5 domain of CheA.
evidence: This is a statement about the predicted structure of ParP based on sequence analysis.

claim: The highly conserved protein interaction tip within the MCP signaling domain is responsible for interactions with CheW and CheA-P5 proteins.
source: The highly conserved protein interaction tip within the MCP signaling domain is responsible for interactions with CheW and CheA-P5 proteins (Kremer et al., 1996; Kim et al., 1999; Li et al., 2007, 2011; Li and Hazelbauer, 2011; Briegel et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2012, 2013; Cassidy et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a well-established fact about MCP structure and function supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Several residues in the MCP TM1143 from T. maritima have been shown to be important for interactions with CheW and CheA-P5: L362, L365, N366, and A368.
source: Furthermore, several residues in the MCP TM1143 from T. maritima have been shown to be important for these interactions: L362, L365, N366, and A368 (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is a well-established fact about MCP structure and function supported by the broader context of the manuscript and illustrated in Figure 2F.

claim: The four residues L362, L365, N366, and A368 in MCP TM1143 from T. maritima are conserved in all of the MCPs identified in the two-hybrid screen and all but two putative MCPs found in V. cholerae.
source: Multiple sequence alignment of all predicted V. cholerae MCPs with the sequence of MCP TM1143 from T. maritima, revealed that these four residues are conserved in all of the MCPs identified in the two-hybrid screen and all but two putative MCPs found in V. cholerae (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the sequence alignment shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Three of the four substitutions (L518R, L521R, and N522R) in MCP VC1898 disrupted the capacity of the MCP to interact with CheW1, but not with itself.
source: Three of the four substitutions (L518R, L521R, and N522R) disrupted the capacity of the MCP to interact with CheW1, but not with itself (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the bacterial-two-hybrid experiments shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The same substitutions (L518R, L521R, and N522R) that disrupted MCP-CheW1 interaction also abolished the interaction between the MCP and ParP.
source: Notably, the same substitutions also abolished the interaction between the MCP and ParP (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the bacterial-two-hybrid experiments shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The effect of the MCP variants on their interactions with CheW1 and ParP is likely not due to reduced expression levels of the MCP variants.
source: Since the MCP variants retained the ability to self-interact, the effect on their interactions with CheW1 and ParP is likely not due to reduced expression levels of the MCP variants.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that the MCP variants retained the ability to self-interact.

claim: YFP-ParP no longer formed clusters co-localizing with mCherry-MCP-L518R clusters, but instead localized diffusely in the cytoplasm in 95% of cells.
source: Notably, YFP-ParP no longer formed clusters co-localizing with mCherry-MCP-L518R clusters, but instead localized diffusely in the cytoplasm (Figure 2D) in 95% of cells (Figure 2E), indicating that the L518R substitution abrogates the capacity of YFP-ParP and mCherry-MCP to interact.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the microscopy experiments shown in Figure 2D-E.

claim: The L518R substitution abrogates the capacity of YFP-ParP and mCherry-MCP to interact.
source: Notably, YFP-ParP no longer formed clusters co-localizing with mCherry-MCP-L518R clusters, but instead localized diffusely in the cytoplasm (Figure 2D) in 95% of cells (Figure 2E), indicating that the L518R substitution abrogates the capacity of YFP-ParP and mCherry-MCP to interact.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the microscopy experiments shown in Figure 2D-E.

claim: ParP-AIF targets the same MCP residues that mediate MCP interactions with CheW and CheA.
source: Altogether, these observations suggest that ParP-AIF targets the same MCP residues that mediate MCPinteractions with CheW and CheA, and thus lends support to the idea that ParP is a component of the chemotaxis core unit of signaling arrays.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the bacterial-two-hybrid and microscopy experiments.

claim: ParP-AIF domains form their own distinct clade of SH3-domains, and are more similar to the P5 domain of CheAs than to CheWs.
source: While ParP-AIF domains form their own distinct clade of SH3-domains, they are more similar to the P5 domain of CheAs than to CheWs (Figure 3A).
